Section: PRE-WRITING AUDIT RESOLUTION

Before drafting, the following corrections identified in Check 1 were verified against the source documents and applied throughout:

22. **£800,000 announcement**: Verified in Barry Born 2025, p. 18. Retained.

text:
Case study: East Riding Managed Retreat (East Riding of Yorkshire, UK)
Section: CASE STUDY OVERVIEW

**Case Name and Location:** Holderness coastline, East Riding of Yorkshire, northeast of England, United Kingdom.

**Hazard(s):** Coastal erosion is the primary hazard driving managed retreat decisions. The Holderness coastline is composed of soft boulder clay deposited during the last ice age, which erodes rapidly under wave action, tidal forces, and rainwater percolation. Historical records indicate average rates of around 1.5–2 metres per year, with some periods and locations experiencing faster loss (Barry Born 2025). Rising sea levels and intensifying storms, associated with climate change, are described in the sources as accelerating these trends. Coastal flooding is a related but secondary concern, addressed separately through hard defences in protected areas.

**Type of Retreat:** This case involves two overlapping mechanisms. The first is an informal, ad hoc practice sometimes called "roll-back," in which individual residential and agricultural properties are demolished and sometimes relocated further inland as they approach the cliff edge — historically with little or no financial support and no standard compensation scheme. The second is the Coastal Transition Accelerator Programme (CTAP), a national programme announced in March 2022 and funded by the Environment Agency (EA) at £36 million total, which aims to pilot more proactive and planned approaches to coastal transition, including roll-back support, infrastructure repurposing, new housing inland, and innovative financial models. An earlier initiative, the Flood Resilience Community Pathfinder scheme (2012–2015), introduced limited compensation for some properties in East Riding, representing a modest earlier attempt at more structured support.

**Scale:** The four stretches of the Holderness coastline designated as "No Active Intervention" (NAI) by the local Shoreline Management Plan are estimated by One Home to contain 648 properties (including caravans) with a combined value of approximately £93 million currently likely to be lost to erosion by 2100 (Barry Born 2025). More than 148 houses and one hotel are at risk over the next 100 years (Thaler 2021). Under the Pathfinder scheme (2012–2015), more than 43 properties were relocated in East Riding (Thaler 2021). The four affected administrative wards — East Wolds and Coastal, North Holderness, Mid Holderness, and South East Holderness — have a combined population of approximately 53,759 and approximately 23,772 households (calculated by summing ward figures from Barry Born 2025, based on 2022 ONS population estimates and 2021 Census data). Not all of these residents are directly in NAI zones facing imminent risk; only a subset are at near-term erosion risk.

**Key Actors:** The Environment Agency (EA) made the £36 million investment in CTAP. Shoreline Management Plans (SMPs) are developed through a partnership of the EA, local authorities, and key stakeholders (Barry Born 2025). East Riding of Yorkshire Council (ERYC) issues eviction notices when the 9.36-metre threshold is crossed and implements local responses to erosion risk, including limited roll-back assistance and the more recent housing initiative. Defra funded the earlier Pathfinder scheme (2012–2015). One Home, a UK-based NGO, has mapped at-risk properties and campaigns for stronger protections and compensation. Individual homeowners are largely expected to manage and fund their own relocation and demolition, with limited and uneven public support.

**Timeline:** Informal, ad hoc relocations in East Riding have occurred since at least the 1970s–1980s, with single houses moved further inland (Thaler 2021). SMPs were established in the 2000s with short- (2005–2025), medium- (2026–2055), and long-term (2056–2100) planning horizons. The Pathfinder scheme ran from 2012 to 2015. CTAP was announced in March 2022. The council began outreach to local residents in late 2023, although many residents had still not heard about CTAP by the time of the 2024 research (Barry Born 2025). In February 2025, East Riding of Yorkshire Council announced £800,000 as part of its Changing Coast East Riding project to develop new housing on the site of derelict agricultural buildings inland to rehouse displaced residents (Barry Born 2025, p. 18). The case is best described as **ongoing**, with CTAP representing the most recent and more proactive planning initiative, though still early-stage.

**Key Outcomes:** The long-standing ad hoc roll-back approach has resulted in sporadic, piecemeal individual relocations over several decades, widely criticised for its lack of compensation, inadequate support, and individualisation of costs onto homeowners — many of whom are elderly. The Pathfinder scheme (2012–2015) provided some improvement by introducing limited compensation for properties at imminent risk. CTAP represents a significant new investment, but at the time of the reviewed research (2024), many residents were unaware of the programme, engagement had been limited, and the fundamental challenge of how to justly compensate and support people who must leave their homes remained unresolved (Barry Born 2025). Some recent legal challenges to policy have been unsuccessful. A key unresolved issue is the perceived inequity of the current system: while larger towns (Bridlington, Hornsea, Withernsea) and the village of Mappleton are protected by sea defences, smaller settlements in NAI zones receive little protection or compensation, and residents bear demolition costs largely alone.

---

**Narrative Summary:**

The Holderness coastline in East Riding of Yorkshire is one of the fastest eroding coastlines in Europe, losing on average up to four metres per year in some locations due to its soft boulder clay geology. For decades, the UK government's response has been governed by Shoreline Management Plans that designate stretches of coastline as either protected ("Hold the Line") or unprotected ("No Active Intervention" — NAI). In NAI zones, which contain hundreds of homes expected to be lost to the sea by 2100, residents have historically received little support. The approach effectively expects homeowners to relocate once their home comes within 9.36 metres of the cliff edge, at which point the local authority issues an eviction notice. Homeowners are then typically required to pay for their own building's demolition, with only limited and uneven public assistance available. The sources indicate no clear, standardised compensation scheme for property-value loss in the East Riding case. This system has resulted in sporadic, piecemeal individual relocations rather than planned community managed retreat.

The human cost of this approach is significant. Research conducted in 2023–24 found that many residents are older homeowners who moved to the Holderness coast for retirement, drawn by relative affordability, natural beauty, and a slower pace of life (Barry Born 2025). For them, the prospect of losing their home — and their financial security — to erosion is deeply unsettling. The evidence indicates that residents experience erosion as both a slow, pervasive background anxiety and a sudden, stressful process of eviction and forced demolition. Residents tend to feel isolated and geographically dispersed, and face a system that, according to the report, distributes the costs of climate adaptation primarily onto individuals rather than society (Barry Born 2025). Some recent legal challenges and community mobilisations have been unsuccessful. A persistent source of grievance is residents' perception that sea defences protecting larger settlements accelerate erosion in neighbouring unprotected villages, meaning those in undefended areas bear costs for decisions made on behalf of others.

The situation is now at a crossroads. In 2022, the Environment Agency invested £36 million through CTAP in East Riding of Yorkshire and North Norfolk to pilot more proactive and innovative approaches to coastal transition, including exploring new housing models inland, improved financial instruments, and better engagement with affected residents. In February 2025, the council announced £800,000 under its Changing Coast East Riding project to develop new housing for displaced residents. However, at the time of the reviewed research (2024), many residents were unaware of CTAP, engagement had been limited, and the core challenge — how to justly compensate and support those who must leave their homes — remained unresolved (Barry Born 2025). The Holderness case is therefore simultaneously a longstanding example of reactive, individualised managed retreat and an emerging, still early-stage test case for more proactive, equitable coastal transition.

---

text:
Case study: East Riding Managed Retreat (East Riding of Yorkshire, UK)
Section: CODING QUESTIONS

---

### Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process? (Reactive/Proactive)

**Answer:** Both — **Reactive** (dominant, historical) and **Proactive** (emerging, under CTAP from 2022 onwards).

**Narrative:** The long-standing roll-back approach in East Riding has been fundamentally reactive. Eviction notices are issued only when individual buildings reach within 9.36 metres of the cliff edge, triggering managed retreat of specific properties after erosion has already significantly advanced. Thaler (2021) describes the English approach as one where "people were left alone to deal with ongoing and future hazards" and the decision was "mainly based on CBA" with no standard compensation. Barry Born (2025) documents resident experiences of being informed about the situation only when demolition was imminent — a reactive pattern.

However, CTAP (announced March 2022) and associated local planning work represent a deliberate effort toward more proactive planning. The EA stated that CTAP aims to "set out planning strategies for transition away from affected coastlines and to trial and support innovative interventions on the ground" (Barry Born 2025, p. 8). The council began outreach in late 2023, though many residents still had not heard about CTAP by 2024 (Barry Born 2025). The Pathfinder scheme (2012–2015) also introduced a more forward-looking element, though it remained limited in scope (Thaler 2021).

**Coding rationale:** Both codes apply. Reactive predominates across the historical period of evidence reviewed. Proactive elements are real but limited and still early-stage at the time of the research.

---

### Date, Number of households affected, Number of population affected, Total funding

**Answer:**

- **Date:** Informal, ad hoc roll-back relocations since at least the 1970s–1980s (Thaler 2021); SMPs formalised in the 2000s with short- (2005–2025), medium- (2026–2055), and long-term (2056–2100) planning horizons (Barry Born 2025); Pathfinder scheme 2012–2015 (Thaler 2021); CTAP announced March 2022 (Barry Born 2025); council CTAP outreach began late 2023, with many residents still unaware by 2024 (Barry Born 2025); £800,000 new housing announced February 2025 (Barry Born 2025).

- **Number of households affected:** 648 properties (including caravans) in the four highest-risk Holderness stretches likely to be lost by 2100 (One Home, cited in Barry Born 2025). More than 148 houses and one hotel at risk over 100 years (Thaler 2021). More than 43 properties were relocated under the Flood Resilience Community Pathfinder scheme in East Riding (Thaler 2021).

- **Number of population affected:** Not stated precisely in the sources. The four affected wards have a combined population of approximately 53,759 and approximately 23,772 households (calculated by summing ward figures from Barry Born 2025, citing 2022 ONS estimates and 2021 Census). Only a subset of these are directly in NAI zones facing near-term risk.

- **Total funding:** CTAP: £36 million total EA investment, with East Riding and North Norfolk as key beneficiaries (Barry Born 2025). Pathfinder scheme: total funding not itemised in reviewed sources; individual-level support documented (e.g., Edward received £3,500 plus a re-roofing contribution; Patricia received demolition assistance) (Barry Born 2025). New inland housing under Changing Coast East Riding project: £800,000 (announced February 2025, Barry Born 2025). Withernsea rock armour sea defences (2019): £7 million (a hard defence measure, not managed retreat) (Barry Born 2025). Hull tidal barrier: £42 million (not managed retreat) (Barry Born 2025). One Home estimates the combined value of at-risk Holderness properties at approximately £93 million (cited in Barry Born 2025).

**Uncertainty:** The precise total funding allocated specifically to managed retreat activities (as distinct from coastal defence investment and CTAP overall) is not comprehensively stated in the reviewed sources.

---

### What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process? (Single Hazard/Multiple Hazards)

**Answer:** **Single Hazard** — coastal erosion as the primary driver of NAI-zone managed retreat decisions — with coastal flooding and sea level rise noted as compounding contextual factors.

**Narrative:** The managed retreat decision process in East Riding is driven overwhelmingly by coastal erosion of soft boulder clay cliffs. Barry Born (2025) consistently frames the case around "coastal erosion" as the central driver of NAI-zone designations and eviction processes. Thaler (2021) also describes the English policy as focused on "coastal erosion risk management." Sea level rise and storm surge are mentioned as compounding factors and are driving future projections, and the near-breach of the Hull tidal barrier in 2013 led to significant flood protection investment for 113,000 homes (Barry Born 2025). However, the NAI-zone managed retreat decisions in this case are driven specifically by erosion.

**Coding rationale:** "Single hazard" is the most defensible primary code given that the NAI-zone retreat decisions are driven by erosion. Coastal flooding and sea level rise are acknowledged as contextual accelerants, addressed through separate protective measures in HTL areas. If the codebook's "multiple hazards" definition is applied to include compounding hazards, a secondary note on sea level rise as a worsening driver is warranted, but "Single hazard" is the primary code.

---

### What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process? (Technological Hazard/Natural Hazard)

**Answer:** **Natural Hazard**, with climate change acknowledged as an accelerating driver.

**Narrative:** Coastal erosion of the Holderness coastline is a long-standing natural geological process. Barry Born (2025) traces the geological origins of the coastline to the last ice age (approximately 50,000 years ago) and notes that erosion has been occurring continuously for millennia, with approximately 32 villages lost since Roman times. The erosion results from wave and tidal forces acting on soft boulder clay, compounded by rainwater percolation. Both sources acknowledge that climate change — including rising sea levels and more intense storm events — is accelerating these rates. Barry Born (2025) quotes the Environment Agency's Chief Executive: "climate change means that some of our communities... cannot stay where they are." Thaler (2021) notes that the English decision process considers "how the risk might change in the future based on sea level rise."

There is one unusual local factor: unexploded ordnance from former RAF practice bombing is lodged in the clay cliffs, and detonation by a Ministry of Defence subcontractor is suspected by some residents to further contribute to local erosion rates (Barry Born 2025). However, this remains speculative and is not established as a primary cause.

**Coding rationale:** Natural Hazard is the appropriate code. The underlying process is natural geomorphological erosion. Climate change is an accelerating driver. There is no primary technological or industrial cause.

---

### Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process? (Coastal Flooding/Erosion), (Riverine/Pluvial Flooding), etc.

**Answer:** **Coastal Flooding/Erosion** — specifically coastal erosion as the primary hazard driving managed retreat decisions in NAI zones.

**Narrative:** The codebook defines "Coastal Flooding/Erosion" as "hazards such as storm surge, flooding, sea level rise, and wave erosion that significantly impact coastal regions." All of these elements are present in this case. Barry Born (2025) and Thaler (2021) both focus on coastal erosion as the primary driver. Sea level rise and storm surge are mentioned as compounding factors. The four NAI stretches of the Holderness coastline are the specific geographic areas triggering managed retreat decisions. No other hazard types feature in the managed retreat decision process for this case.

---

### What was the geographic scale of the MR project? (Individual homes), (A few streets), (Neighbourhood), (Entire community), (Sub-watershed), (Watershed region)

**Answer:** **Individual homes** (primary, reflecting actual practice); **A few streets** (secondary, in aggregate in some villages and in some historical examples).

**Narrative:** The roll-back approach has operated primarily at the level of individual homes — properties are dealt with one by one as they reach the 9.36-metre threshold. Thaler (2021) notes "more than 43 properties were relocated in East Riding" under the Pathfinder scheme and that "single houses were relocated" since the 1970s. Barry Born (2025) describes evictions and demolitions of individual houses and farmhouses. However, in at least one documented historical case, an entire road and row of bungalows was rebuilt further inland (Sandra's account, Barry Born 2025), and the pattern of multiple properties in a small village being affected over time constitutes effective street-level impact.

CTAP ambitions include community-led housing approaches and new inland settlements, suggesting a larger scale is envisaged for future phases, but this had not yet been implemented at community scale at the time of the research.

**Coding rationale:** "Individual homes" is the primary code reflecting actual documented practice. "A few streets" applies in aggregate within specific villages and in the whole-road rebuild example. "Neighbourhood" is not coded as a primary scale given the evidence base. "Entire community" does not apply — no whole community has been retreated as a unit.

---

### Who or what was retreated? (Individuals), (Groups/Neighbourhoods), (Communities), (Critical infrastructure), (Hazard protection structures), (Industrial assets)

**Answer:** **Individuals** primarily. Some evidence of **Groups/Neighbourhoods** in specific documented historical cases.

**Narrative:** The evidence consistently describes individual homeowners and, in some cases, farming families as the units of retreat. Barry Born (2025) documents individual eviction notices, individual demolition decisions, and individual relocation decisions. Thaler (2021) confirms that the English policy has operated primarily at the individual property level. The account of Sandra's family — whose whole road and row of bungalows was rebuilt further inland in the 1980s — provides evidence of at least some historical group-level relocation (Barry Born 2025). The CTAP plans for new inland housing for displaced residents suggest emerging group-level planning, but this remained in very early stages at the time of the research. No critical infrastructure, hazard protection structures, or industrial assets are described as the subjects of managed retreat in this case.

---

### Other notes (General Information)

Barry Born (2025) notes that approximately 32 villages have been lost along the Holderness coastline since Roman times, providing important long-term historical context for the case. The presence of unexploded ordnance from former RAF practice bombing in the clay cliffs adds an unusual complicating factor — detonation by a Ministry of Defence subcontractor may further contribute to local erosion rates, according to local residents, though this is speculative (Barry Born 2025). The report also notes traveller occupation of abandoned cliff-edge land as part of the local housing context, adding social complexity to the retreat areas (Barry Born 2025). The case operates within the broader UK context of asset-based welfare, where homeownership is closely tied to financial and ontological security, making the loss of a coastal home particularly destabilising for elderly homeowners.

Of the 21 sections of coastline most at risk of coastal erosion nationally between now and 2100, four are along the Holderness coastline, which together with North Norfolk contain an estimated 84% of all residential properties at risk of coastal erosion in England in the next 20 years, according to an EA press release cited in Barry Born (2025).

---

source: Pipeline Ver2 — East Riding Managed Retreat
text:
Case study: East Riding Managed Retreat (East Riding of Yorkshire, UK)
Section: INSTITUTIONAL ENVIRONMENT

---

### What is the focus or scope of the MR project? (Individual buyout/retreat), (Community buyout/retreat), (Leasebacks, easements and buffers), (Other acquisition tools), (Managed realignment of infrastructure)

**Answer:** **Individual buyout/retreat** (primary, historical); **Other acquisition tools** (buy-back and lease-back arrangements under the Pathfinder scheme); **Community buyout/retreat** is an aspiration under CTAP but not yet realised.

**Narrative:** The primary mode of managed retreat in Holderness has been at the individual level — either through the ad hoc roll-back approach (where individual properties reach the eviction threshold and are demolished) or through the Pathfinder scheme's property-level compensation. Thaler (2021) describes the Pathfinder outcomes as individual property relocations (43 in East Riding). Barry Born (2025) describes "buy-back and lease-back options" offered to properties at lower risk levels under the Pathfinder scheme. These buy-back and leaseback arrangements for lower-risk properties represent an additional acquisition mechanism; the codebook category "Leasebacks, easements and buffers" partly covers this, though there is no specific evidence of formal easement or buffer zone arrangements in this case. "Other acquisition tools" is therefore a more cautious code for the buy-back/leaseback element.

CTAP ambitions, as described by Barry Born (2025), include community-led housing approaches and exploring new inland housing development, suggesting a potential shift toward community-level retreat. The February 2025 £800,000 Changing Coast East Riding housing announcement represents a more community-oriented planning approach. However, this remains nascent and had not resulted in implemented community-level retreat at the time of the research. The codebook defines "Community buyout/retreat" as "collective relocation of a neighborhood or settlement through coordinated planning and community engagement"; this does not yet apply in realised form.

**Coding rationale:** "Individual buyout/retreat" applies to both the historical roll-back period and the Pathfinder period. "Other acquisition tools" is coded for the buy-back/leaseback arrangements. "Community buyout/retreat" is noted only as an emerging aspiration under CTAP, not as a current practice.

---

### What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process?

**Answer:** **Relevant regulations/acts**, **Legal authority over retreat**, **Home acquisition**, **Retreat land development** (partial), **Compliance & enforcement**, and **Litigation**. Elements of **Land rezoning** are present only in de facto restriction form, not as a formal rezoning process.

**Narrative:**

- **Relevant regulations/acts:** SMPs provide the overarching planning framework. Barry Born (2025, p. 8) explicitly states that "SMPs have neither legal status nor funding." The former means development can continue in NAI areas despite SMP designation; the latter means HTL or MR areas may in practice become NAI over time. This non-binding nature of SMPs is a critical legal gap. Thaler (2021) notes that the integrated coastal zone management plan governs English managed retreat decisions.

- **Legal authority over retreat:** The local authority (East Riding of Yorkshire Council) holds the authority to issue eviction notices once the 9.36-metre threshold is crossed (Barry Born 2025). This authority is real but constrained by the non-binding nature of SMPs and the absence of a statutory compensation framework.

- **Home acquisition:** The Pathfinder scheme introduced buy-back options for properties. The roll-back approach offers residents the opportunity to purchase and redevelop land further inland at a subsidised price, though this has not been widely taken up due to the significant capital required (Barry Born 2025). Thaler (2021) notes that "before the Flood Resilience Community Pathfinder scheme, the government did not predict any compensation strategy in the East Riding example."

- **Retreat land development:** The SMP technically permits continued development in NAI areas given the absence of legal status, creating a potentially maladaptive dynamic (Barry Born 2025). New construction on NAI coastline "happens on an ad hoc basis" (Barry Born 2025, p. 18).

- **Land rezoning:** There is no documented formal rezoning process in England comparable to the Austrian model (where residential land is reclassified to grassland). Thaler (2021) notes that England involves "restriction of future use of the owned land/or loss of planning permission and legal agreements" — a de facto restriction rather than formal rezoning. This is coded cautiously.

- **Compliance & enforcement:** Residents are required to demolish buildings when instructed by the council. John's account (Barry Born 2025) describes council pressure to demolish outbuildings, with the council threatening to "send somebody in and charge you for it."

- **Litigation:** Elaine took the local authority to court but was ultimately unsuccessful (Barry Born 2025). A separate case — a disabled man in Hemsby, Norfolk supported by Friends of the Earth — challenged the government's National Adaptation Plan 3 as insufficient and unlawful; the case was unsuccessful (October 2024, Barry Born 2025). These represent genuine legal challenges to managed retreat policy.

**Coding rationale:** Multiple categories apply. The absence of a standardised compensation framework and the non-binding status of SMPs are the most significant legal constraints identified. "Land rezoning" is treated cautiously and not coded as a formal process.

---

### What were the funding sources for the MR project?

**Answer:** **Multiple funders**: primarily **Federal** (national government — EA/Defra) with **Local/Municipal** co-implementation; **Individual** contribution also significant.

**Narrative:** The CTAP fund of £36 million is a national Environment Agency initiative — central government (federal-level in UK context) funding (Barry Born 2025). The Pathfinder scheme (2012–2015) was a Defra national initiative (Thaler 2021). East Riding of Yorkshire Council administers programmes and co-invests; the £800,000 Changing Coast East Riding housing project (announced February 2025) is a local authority investment (Barry Born 2025).

Critically, individual homeowners are expected to bear a significant portion of costs themselves, including demolition costs. Barry Born (2025) documents Elaine's family paying approximately £30,000 for asbestos removal. Edward received £3,500 and a re-roofing contribution from the council under the Pathfinder scheme, while Patricia received demolition cost assistance she could not otherwise have afforded (Barry Born 2025). The roll-back offer requires significant capital from homeowners even when subsidised. Insurance for erosion-affected properties is described as essentially unavailable (One Home, cited in Barry Born 2025).

**Coding rationale:** "Multiple funders" applies (Federal/national + Local/Municipal). "Individual" also applies given the significant personal costs borne by homeowners. Insurance is explicitly noted as unavailable. No NGO or international aid funding for this managed retreat process is identified.

---

### What was considered to maintain (or improve) the tax base in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Limited evidence. Some emerging elements of **New housing for BO recipients** (the February 2025 Changing Coast East Riding housing announcement). Tax base considerations are not explicitly discussed as a stated goal in the reviewed sources.

**Narrative:** Barry Born (2025) notes that the February 2025 announcement of £800,000 for new housing on the site of derelict agricultural buildings inland represents an attempt to provide housing for displaced residents — the plan encompasses two- and three-bedroom housing for social rent or shared ownership. This could be interpreted as a modest effort to retain residents in the local area. However, neither source explicitly discusses maintaining or enhancing the tax base as a stated goal of the managed retreat programme.

Thaler (2021) briefly notes that English coastal areas subject to NAI "typically rural, densely populated [sic — sparsely populated]... have low economic activities, which usually create a lower benefit-cost ratio with the implications that the public administration does not provide any structural protection schemes." This suggests economic decline is a recognised challenge but is not actively addressed through a tax-base strategy in the retreat programme. Barry Born (2025) mentions caravan parks as a lucrative land use that may replace lost residential properties, but this is not described as a planned municipal strategy.

**Coding rationale:** "New housing for BO recipients" is the most applicable code, emerging under the 2025 Changing Coast East Riding initiative. No explicit tax base maintenance strategy is identified in the reviewed sources. This is a notable gap in programme design.

---

### What level/type of compensation mechanisms were considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Historically: **no compensation** (pre-Pathfinder). Under the Pathfinder scheme (2012–2015): limited **Additional incentives, bonuses and top-ups** (hardship payments, agent fees) and **Free supports and services** (demolition cost subsidies). Buy-back and leaseback options are documented but fell short of full market-value compensation in practice.

**Narrative:** Thaler (2021) is explicit that "the English managed retreat policy did not include a clear, standardised approach for compensating private land owners" and that "before the Flood Resilience Community Pathfinder scheme, the government did not predict any compensation strategy in the East Riding example." The sources indicate no clear, standardised compensation scheme for property-value loss in the East Riding case. This distinguishes England sharply from Austria (80% of time-value of building + 80% of demolition costs under Austrian policy, per Thaler 2021).

Under the Pathfinder scheme in East Riding:
- Properties at Level 1 (imminent) risk could apply for "small hardship payments" and "payment of agent fees" (Thaler 2021).
- Properties at lower risk levels were offered "buy-back and lease-back options" (Thaler 2021).
- East Riding differentiated compensation by risk level; Waveney differentiated by year of building construction (Thaler 2021).

Barry Born (2025) documents individual experiences: Edward received £3,500 and a re-roofing contribution under the Pathfinder scheme; Patricia received demolition assistance she could not otherwise afford; John found the support offered felt like an "insult." The roll-back offer — subsidised purchase of land further inland — constitutes an additional incentive but requires significant capital from the homeowner and has not been widely taken up.

**Coding rationale:** "Additional incentives, bonuses and top-ups" (hardship payments, agent fees) and "Free supports and services" (demolition subsidies, limited relocation assistance) apply for the Pathfinder period. The buy-back/
